frase_gancho.texto: A stone cylinder that slept for almost five hundred years beneath the center of the city.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the cylinder of the captives we move on to another vessel for offerings, this time shaped like an animal. Walk toward the stone jaguar that comes next: on its back there is a hollow made to receive hearts.

guion_corto.texto: Eleven scenes of conquest wrap around this stone cylinder. In every one the same image repeats: a ruler, wearing the insignia of a god, grips a defeated warrior by the hair, and beside each vanquished man appears the glyph of his people. This is the Stone of the Former Archbishopric, a Mexica work discovered in 1988, during construction on Moneda Street, in the center of Mexico City. Some specialists link it to Motecuhzoma Ilhuicamina, the tlatoani who ruled before Tízoc. On the upper face there is a solar disk with a face at its center. It is thought to have been used for ritual combat and to receive offerings of blood and hearts.

guion_largo.texto:
Sometimes archaeology doesn’t begin with an expedition, but with a trench. In 1988, during foundation work on an old building on Moneda Street, in the Historic Center of Mexico City, workers came upon a large round stone. It was still in place, a short distance from the Templo Mayor, at the spot where the Mexica had set it almost five hundred years earlier.

The building was the former Archbishop’s Palace, and that is why the piece bears that name, even though there is nothing colonial about it. Its land was part of the Sacred Precinct of Tenochtitlan, the ceremonial heart of the Mexica capital. For centuries, the modern city grew on top of a monument that no one knew was there.

It is a wide, low cylinder of basalt, more than two meters in diameter. If you walk around it, you will see eleven nearly identical scenes, separated by a band that repeats the same motif. In each one, a ruler grips a defeated warrior by the hair. Seizing someone by the hair was the gesture of total victory. Beside each captive there is a glyph, the name of his people; according to some studies, among them appear peoples of the Valley of Mexico such as Chalco or Xochimilco.

The ruler wears the insignia of a god. Iconographic studies identify his attire with that of Xiuhtecuhtli, the god of fire; other specialists read him as Tezcatlipoca. It doesn’t matter so much which: the king does not present himself as an ordinary man, but as a god who subdues his enemies.

And who is the king? Some researchers believe he is Motecuhzoma Ilhuicamina, the fifth tlatoani, who ruled from 1440 to 1469. If so, this stone predates the Stone of Tízoc, the one you have just seen. The two share the same idea: a list of victories that was also an offering table.

If you could peer onto the upper face, you would see a solar disk. In the central hollow there is a human face, that of the Sun, and around it, borders with the symbols of sacrifice: skulls, crossed bones, hearts, hands and knives. The stone is thought to have served as a temalácatl, a platform for ritual combat, and as a cuauhxicalli, a vessel for the hearts and blood offered to the Sun.

Those rites are connected to Tlacaxipehualiztli, the spring festival dedicated to [Xipe Tótec](mna_s04_xipe_totec), the god of skin whom you saw in the Teotihuacán Hall. In Nahuatl, the name of the festival means something like “the flaying of people.” It is a harsh word, and it should be understood in its context: for the Mexica, that festival was part of the renewal of the earth.

There is a curious coincidence. The [Stone of Tízoc](mna_s06_tizoc) appeared in 1791, during work in the Plaza Mayor; the Archbishopric stone, in 1988, also during construction, a few streets away. Almost two hundred years separate the two discoveries, and in both cases the modern city stumbled upon the past while digging.

As you walk away, think about this: beneath the streets where you walk there are still more pieces waiting. The city, even today, is still searching for them.

texto: Count the scenes of conquest that surround the cylinder
Find the ruler gripping a warrior by the hair
Look at the borders: there are skulls, hearts, hands and knives

texto.Period: Late Postclassic (around 1440-1469 AD, reign of Motecuhzoma Ilhuicamina)
texto.Material: Basalt carved in high relief (11 scenes of conquest)
texto.Origin: Former Archbishop’s Palace, 4 Moneda Street, Historic Center, Mexico City (found in 1988)
texto.Dimensions: 72 cm high x 224 cm in diameter

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Stone of the Former Archbishopric is another Aztec calendar, like the Sun Stone.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is not a calendar. It is a monument to conquest: its eleven scenes show the victories of a Mexica ruler.
